topic: What should go into AI-coding-harness root context/instruction files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules, .windsurfrules, CONVENTIONS.md, copilot-instructions.md, GEMINI.md) to be maximally useful, and what content is harmful/redundant/wasteful
plan: What is the purpose/mental model of these files (system-prompt injection vs README vs constitution)?
Which content categories have documented positive impact, and from which source?
Which content categories are documented as harmful/wasteful?
What concrete empirical findings exist on instruction-following degradation / context rot / lost-in-the-middle as these files grow?
What structure/ordering is recommended (progressive disclosure, imports, monorepo nesting, token-budget guidance)?
How do the harnesses differ / where can recommendations be harness-agnostic vs harness-specific?

sections.title: Purpose and mental model
sections.summary: These files are best modeled as an auto-injected, low-trust context/system-prompt addendum re-sent every session -- not a persistent memory, not a human README, and (per Claude Code specifically) not even binding instructions the model must obey. LLMs are stateless between sessions; the root file is the primary default mechanism for carrying project-specific knowledge into a fresh context window. Multiple harnesses (AGENTS.md consortium, Cursor) explicitly separate this file from README.md: README is for humans, the root context file is for agents and can contain build/test/convention detail that would clutter a human-facing README.

claims.text: LLMs are stateless between sessions; the root context file is the primary default mechanism to carry project knowledge into every fresh context window, since coding agents 'know absolutely nothing about your codebase at the beginning of each session.'
claims.verificationNote: Independently stated by Anthropic's own memory architecture (fresh context window each session, two mechanisms carry knowledge across) and by HumanLayer's practitioner analysis.

sections.title: Content categories documented as harmful or wasteful
sections.summary: Convergent, cross-vendor evidence: content the agent can already derive by reading the code (directory layout, dependency lists, architecture overviews it will discover in seconds), generic/self-evident advice the model already knows from training or the harness's own system prompt, and excessive length/redundant instructions, all measurably reduce task success and/or raise cost -- this is not merely 'wasted tokens,' it is documented as actively harmful.

claims.text: Content the agent can derive by reading the code (directory layout, dependency lists, file-by-file descriptions, architecture overviews) is explicitly flagged as exclude-worthy and, per an academic study, is exactly the boilerplate that dominates auto-generated context files without adding value.
claims.verificationNote: Four independent sources converge: Anthropic's own ✅/❌ table, Anthropic's shipped '/doctor' trim tool, Cursor's official docs, and the ETH Zurich/LogicStar.ai AgentBench study.

sections.title: Empirical findings on instruction-following degradation, context rot, and big-file benchmarks
sections.summary: Two distinct but converging empirical strands: (1) general 'context rot' research (Chroma) showing LLM accuracy declines as input length and distractor count grow, extending the older 'Lost in the Middle' finding beyond simple retrieval; (2) context-file-specific research (ETH Zurich/LogicStar.ai's AgentBench paper, plus an independent community benchmark) showing that both auto-generated and even most hand-written CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md files fail to reliably improve, and often hurt, coding-agent task success -- with a documented counter-example (Arize) showing gains are achievable when instructions are iteratively optimized against real failure signal rather than written once by intuition.

claims.text: Adding even a single distractor to a long-context task reduces model accuracy relative to a clean-needle baseline, and this degradation compounds with more distractors; distractors do not have uniform impact (some hurt far more than others).
claims.verificationNote: Single-origin (Chroma Research's own study); no independently-run replication found in this pass, though it builds on and is broadly consistent with the older, separately-authored Liu et al. 2023 'Lost in the Middle' line of work referenced across multiple secondary sources.

sources.title: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance

claims.text: In Chroma's 18-model evaluation, models that scored above 95% accuracy on short-input tasks fell to roughly 60-70% as input length grew into the thousands of tokens with semantically-relevant distractor content present.

sections.title: Recommended structure, progressive disclosure, and token-budget guidance
sections.summary: Every harness with an import/reference mechanism (Claude Code @path, Gemini CLI @file.md) explicitly documents that imports help organization but do NOT reduce context cost, since imported content loads at launch alongside the root file -- the actual context-reduction mechanism is path-scoped/glob-conditional rules (Claude Code path-scoped rules, Cursor globs, Copilot applyTo, Windsurf glob-activation), which load only when matching files are touched. Monorepos should use nested per-package files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md all support this), with the closest file to the working directory taking precedence. There is no single universal token-budget number -- each vendor/format publishes its own threshold, and the trend across nearly all of them is toward 'as short as possible,' not a fixed target.

claims.text: @path-style imports (Claude Code) and @file.md imports (Gemini CLI) help organize a large file into smaller pieces, but do NOT reduce the context actually sent to the model -- imported files are expanded and loaded at launch alongside the referencing file. To actually reduce context cost (not just organize), use path-scoped/glob-conditional rules instead, a pattern independently implemented across at least four harnesses.
claims.verificationNote: Strongly corroborated: the 'imports don't reduce context' caveat is Claude Code's own explicit documentation; the 'use conditional/glob rules instead' pattern is independently implemented by Cursor (globs), GitHub Copilot (applyTo frontmatter on *.instructions.md), and Windsurf/Devin (glob activation mode).

sections.title: Cross-harness differences and compatibility notes
sections.summary: AGENTS.md is the closest thing to a cross-tool standard (backed by OpenAI, Google, Cursor, Factory, Sourcegraph per its own site); every other filename is a harness-specific binding onto broadly the same underlying pattern. Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf/Devin, and Gemini CLI all support directory-hierarchy discovery and a conditional/glob-scoped loading mode; GitHub Copilot layers repo-wide + path-scoped + AGENTS.md instructions with explicit precedence; Aider is the outlier -- it has no automatic root-file discovery at all and instead requires the user to explicitly /read or config-load a CONVENTIONS.md as a read-only, cache-friendly context block.

claims.text: Claude Code natively reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md. The documented bridge pattern is a CLAUDE.md whose first line is an @AGENTS.md import (or running /init in a repo that already has an AGENTS.md), leveraging Claude Code's own import mechanism.

claims.text: Aider is the outlier: it has no automatic project-root convention-file discovery. The user must explicitly load a CONVENTIONS.md via /read or the read: key in .aider.conf.yml, at which point it is treated as read-only and cached (if prompt caching is enabled) rather than injected as mutable memory.
claims.verificationNote: Single primary source (Aider's own official docs); this is the authoritative source for Aider's own behavior so corroboration from a second vendor is not applicable/expected.

sources.title: Specifying coding conventions | aider

contradictions.field: Does static context-file content measurably improve coding-agent task success?

candidates.claim: Static human-written and LLM-generated context files provide, at best, marginal (+4%) gains and often measurably hurt (-2 to -3% for LLM-generated, all instruction profiles below empty-file baseline in the 1,188-test benchmark)
candidates.source: ETH Zurich/LogicStar.ai AgentBench paper + independent community 1,188-test benchmark

candidates.claim: Iteratively-optimized, failure-driven instructions (Arize's Prompt Learning) gained +5.19% to +10.87% on SWE-bench splits with zero architecture change

contradictions.delta: Direction reverses depending on how the instructions were produced (one-shot human/LLM authoring vs iterative optimization against real failure signal)
contradictions.winner: Context-dependent, not a true factual conflict: both findings are plausibly correct under their respective methodologies -- static, generically-written or LLM-boilerplate files tend to hurt or barely help, while instructions specifically derived from and validated against the target model's actual failure modes can help. The practical implication (see include/exclude sections) is that only non-obvious, failure-correcting content earns its place in the file; generic or derivable content does not, regardless of who or what wrote it.
